2,886 After my sophomore year, I was outside the training facility in tears — calling my mom, ready to transfer and leave it all behind. They wouldn't play me where I wanted. I wasn't getting the minutes I felt I deserved. I was watching guys in my recruiting class earn All-Big 10 honors as freshmen and I felt stuck. My parents told me one thing: "Stick it out. Get your hands in the dirt." So I stayed. Someone handed me a book that completely changed my mindset — and everything shifted from there. My training. My habits. My routines. My focus. And the confidence I built by pushing through the hardest moment of my career? That was worth more than taking the easy road. Every time you do something hard and see it through — you prove to yourself who you really are. 💪 #soccer #grit #growthmindset #resilience #neverquit
547 I needed to remind myself this one
2,820 5 Big ones that will open your life to new possibilities 🌱 1. Stop waiting for permission — build the life you want. 2. Comfort is a slow kind of death — choose the what you know is the right thing no matter how hard it seems 3. People leave; your standards shouldn’t. 🪞 4. Living your dream will give the people you love permission to do the same. 🍃 5. Fear is a compass, not a jail cell — follow it toward growth.
476 What soccer taught me… I carry into everything I do. Fitness isn’t about motivation. It’s about showing up when you don’t feel like it. Staying consistent when nothing is changing. And not quitting on yourself. That’s the difference.

1,404 I went to train today… just for fun. And I didn’t expect it to hit me like that. This sport has been part of my life since I was 9 years old. It shaped me into who I am today. And when it was over… it was hard. I had to find myself again. Reinvent who I was without soccer. Figure out what was next. That’s why I understand the struggle… that feeling of “now what?” But today reminded me of something. I didn’t realize how much I missed it. Because the moment I step on the field… I don’t think about anything else. I’m just there. Fully present. Soccer gives me a kind of honest joy I can’t even explain. It calms me, grounds me… it feels like home. And if I’m who I am today… it’s because of this sport. ⚽️
1,011 Chasing something bigger than comfort. It gets hard. It gets lonely. But it’s worth it. The job is NOT finished… #australia #newbeginnings #soccerlife #footballjourney #motivation

251 I got cut from my Soccer team. Lost all my friends. And the one girl that still mattered to me left. I was in so much pain but I couldn’t even stomach what to say, I felt like a failure. I started internalizing everything so I looked strong on the outside but that only made it worse. My life stopped becoming something I experienced and became something I just survived. Reflecting opened the gate that kept me stuck. DM me POTENTIAL to build purpose through physique transformation.
368 I tried so hard that I became delusional to the idea that there was even a world outside of soccer. And when it was all taken away, what I was left with wasn’t accomplishment. It was nothing. Like everything had been stripped away from me. #soccer #identity #cut #effort #pain
368 I’m just happy to be here

4,226 We often look for happiness in our goals and the final destination when we spend 95% of the time in the pursuit. If we really set our lives up in that way and ignore the process and don’t actively try to create a process we love just as much then we’re pretty much accepting that we will be unhappy 95% of the time. For me in football this is the mindset I had for a long time I was chasing a dream and I wasn’t going to be happy until I reached it but along the way after hitting certain goals I realised that the happiness I felt only lasted for a short time and I’d put all that hard work and sacrifice for a moment of happiness. Since then I’ve slowly started to realise that by living in the moment and enjoying each day and finding the love for what I do on the journey to each destination has allowed me to feel a lot more fulfilled and at peace and actually lead me to more progress because I was free from being dragged by one goal to the next rather than actively and purposely taking myself there instead
528 Why I love sport & why I look for competitive people to work with in my team… There is nothing like competition. Source: https://www.usaluge.org/news/2023/december/04/2018-olympic-silver-medalist-chris-mazdzer-announces-retirement-
Title: 2018 Olympic Silver Medalist Chris Mazdzer announces retirement
Chunks: 0,1,2
LAKE PLACID, N.Y. —Four-time Olympian and 2018 Olympic silver medalist Chris Mazdzer today announced his retirement from competitive luge. Following an esteemed 22-year career of competing internationally in the sport, Mazdzer has decided the EBERSPAECHER Luge World Cup taking place in Lake Placid on December 8-9 will be his last.
Mazdzer, who grew up in Saranac Lake, N.Y., and now resides in Salt Lake City, Utah, rose to international prominence following the 2018 Winter Games in PyeongChang, where he became the first U.S. men’s singles luge athlete to earn an Olympic medal, which also cemented him as the only non-European to win a medal in the event.
Over his career, he was a seven-time national champion, collected 24 World Cup medals, one World Championship, an Olympic silver medal, and finished third overall in the 2015-16 World Cup standings. In addition to singles racing, he teamed up with two-time Olympian Jayson Terdiman in 2019 to compete in men’s doubles. Mazdzer and Terdiman helped the U.S. team win a bronze medal at the 2020 World Championships.
Mazdzer is one of the select few athletes to have won a World Cup medal in both singles and doubles.
Off the ice, he served his fellow teammates and competitors as an athlete representative at all levels within the sport. He helped establish the Athlete Commission at the Federation of International Luge (FIL) and was the first athlete representative voted by his peers to sit on the FIL board of directors, where he served two consecutive four-year terms. Mazdzer currently serves on the USA Luge board of directors and is the primary representative to the Team USA Athlete Commission.
“Chris began sliding with USA Luge when he was eight years old and over the years his commitment to the sport has been unwavering,” said Jim Leahy, CEO, USA Luge. “Following the 2018 Games, Chris’ success helped raise awareness of the sport across the country. While we will miss Chris as a dedicated athlete, we are grateful for his many successful years and wish him all the best in his next endeavor.”

Of his retirement, Mazdzer said: “After 25 incredible years of hurtling myself down icy chutes in a spandex suit, I realize that every adrenaline-packed career eventually comes to an end. As I hang up my sled and look back at my luge journey, it's clear that this sport has been the greatest teacher in my life, shaping me in ways I never thought possible.
“A few weeks ago, as I made the decision that Lake Placid would be my last World Cup, I felt mixed emotions. It's hard not to feel a little bit of sadness bidding farewell to a sport that I love so dearly. From the exhilarating feeling of being out of control at 90 MPH, to the incredible friendships and camaraderie forged while traversing the globe, luge has changed me for the better. But I am so excited to be raising a family and the doors that will open after I close the door on this incredible chapter in my life.
“First and foremost, I owe a massive thank you to the real MVPs – my friends and family. While luge may be an individual sport, there's no denying that your unwavering love and support have been a huge part of my success. Thank you for traveling the globe to cheer me on in my quest to be the world's best sledder.
“To my fellow lugers, coaches, and teammates, what a ride it's been! From the rollercoaster of laughs and late nights spent in windowless sled rooms, to the highs, lows, and everything in between, you've been my second family for the past two decades. I'll miss the camaraderie and the countless moments that cameras couldn't capture but will forever be etched in our memories.
“As I bid farewell, I carry with me a treasure trove of memories and moments with all of you that I'll cherish forever. Reflecting on my career, I hope I achieved my two goals: leaving the sport better than I found it and increasing awareness of luge in the United States. While I can't objectively answer those questions, I feel a sense of accomplishment in these endeavors.

“Looking ahead, I am genuinely excited for the future of USA Luge. There are phenomenal athletes on the horizon, and I can't wait to watch them this season and in the seasons to come. The momentum behind the scenes is exciting, and while it's going to be challenging not to be directly involved, I am eager to witness the continued success and growth of the sport.
“Again, thank you to my family, friends, teammates, sponsors, coaches, USA Luge staff, Athletic Trainers, training partners, competitors, fans, and so much more for being part of this incredible journey. Here's to the next thrilling chapter!”

LAKE PLACID, N.Y. —Four-time Olympian and 2018 Olympic silver medalist Chris Mazdzer today announced his retirement from competitive luge. Following an esteemed 22-year career of competing internationally in the sport, Mazdzer has decided the EBERSPAECHER Luge World Cup taking place in Lake Placid on December 8-9 will be his last.
Mazdzer, who grew up in Saranac Lake, N.Y., and now resides in Salt Lake City, Utah, rose to international prominence following the 2018 Winter Games in PyeongChang, where he became the first U.S. men’s singles luge athlete to earn an Olympic medal, which also cemented him as the only non-European to win a medal in the event.
Over his career, he was a seven-time national champion, collected 24 World Cup medals, one World Championship, an Olympic silver medal, and finished third overall in the 2015-16 World Cup standings. In addition to singles racing, he teamed up with two-time Olympian Jayson Terdiman in 2019 to compete in men’s doubles. Mazdzer and Terdiman helped the U.S. team win a bronze medal at the 2020 World Championships.
Mazdzer is one of the select few athletes to have won a World Cup medal in both singles and doubles.
Off the ice, he served his fellow teammates and competitors as an athlete representative at all levels within the sport. He helped establish the Athlete Commission at the Federation of International Luge (FIL) and was the first athlete representative voted by his peers to sit on the FIL board of directors, where he served two consecutive four-year terms. Mazdzer currently serves on the USA Luge board of directors and is the primary representative to the Team USA Athlete Commission.
“Chris began sliding with USA Luge when he was eight years old and over the years his commitment to the sport has been unwavering,” said Jim Leahy, CEO, USA Luge. “Following the 2018 Games, Chris’ success helped raise awareness of the sport across the country. While we will miss Chris as a dedicated athlete, we are grateful for his many successful years and wish him all the best in his next endeavor.”
texts.1:
Of his retirement, Mazdzer said: “After 25 incredible years of hurtling myself down icy chutes in a spandex suit, I realize that every adrenaline-packed career eventually comes to an end. As I hang up my sled and look back at my luge journey, it's clear that this sport has been the greatest teacher in my life, shaping me in ways I never thought possible.
“A few weeks ago, as I made the decision that Lake Placid would be my last World Cup, I felt mixed emotions. It's hard not to feel a little bit of sadness bidding farewell to a sport that I love so dearly. From the exhilarating feeling of being out of control at 90 MPH, to the incredible friendships and camaraderie forged while traversing the globe, luge has changed me for the better. But I am so excited to be raising a family and the doors that will open after I close the door on this incredible chapter in my life.
“First and foremost, I owe a massive thank you to the real MVPs – my friends and family. While luge may be an individual sport, there's no denying that your unwavering love and support have been a huge part of my success. Thank you for traveling the globe to cheer me on in my quest to be the world's best sledder.
“To my fellow lugers, coaches, and teammates, what a ride it's been! From the rollercoaster of laughs and late nights spent in windowless sled rooms, to the highs, lows, and everything in between, you've been my second family for the past two decades. I'll miss the camaraderie and the countless moments that cameras couldn't capture but will forever be etched in our memories.
“As I bid farewell, I carry with me a treasure trove of memories and moments with all of you that I'll cherish forever. Reflecting on my career, I hope I achieved my two goals: leaving the sport better than I found it and increasing awareness of luge in the United States. While I can't objectively answer those questions, I feel a sense of accomplishment in these endeavors.
texts.2:
“Looking ahead, I am genuinely excited for the future of USA Luge. There are phenomenal athletes on the horizon, and I can't wait to watch them this season and in the seasons to come. The momentum behind the scenes is exciting, and while it's going to be challenging not to be directly involved, I am eager to witness the continued success and growth of the sport.
“Again, thank you to my family, friends, teammates, sponsors, coaches, USA Luge staff, Athletic Trainers, training partners, competitors, fans, and so much more for being part of this incredible journey. Here's to the next thrilling chapter!”

The Two-time Olympic qualifier and Swiss Record holder was one of the first swimmers to retire this year, with news of Ugolkova’s retirement breaking just after the New Year. Throughout her career, Ugolkova held 19 Swiss records and competed at the Olympics in 2016 and 2021.
